new_statements.citation: Headland, Thomas N. 2003. Thirty endangered languages in the Philippines. Work Papers of the SIL, University of North Dakota Session 47.
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed and it was checked in full (all 13 PDF pages a full-text search for stress/accent terms: none). Spot-checked the other on-disk files in the folder, none of them listed works: no 'stress'/'accent' anywhere; Dicamay appears only in fn. 2 as an extinct group), Table 3.2 and pp. 66, 96-97: Dicamay listed extinct, 'neither of which I have any other information about', re-quotes Headland), Table 2 cognate percentage 60% and map code only). Nothing on stress for Dicamay Agta was missed.

sources.citation: Headland, Thomas N. & Alan Healey. 1974. Grammatical sketch of Casiguran Dumagat. Papers in Philippine Linguistics 6, Pacific Linguistics A-43, 1-54. Canberra: ANU. Table 2 (p.3), map code (p.4).
sources.note: Phonology section is for Casiguran Dumagat only. Dicamay appears solely as a lexicostatistic figure, 'Casiguran Dumagat - Dicamay Negrito 60%' (Table 2, p.3), and as map code 10 'area of Dicamay Negrito speakers' (p.4) — evidently computed from Roe's wordlist. No Dicamay phonological or stress data.

sources.citation: Pelila, John Rey Osben, Shirley Lacson Ayao-ao & Maureen Bolante Casiano. 2023. If these languages could talk: the extinct languages of the Philippines. International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Publications (IJMRAP) 6(3): 127-134. Saint Louis University, Baguio City.
sources.note: Nothing. A document review of four extinct Philippine languages (Agta Dicamay, Agta Villa Viciosa, Ayta Tayabas, Katabaga); the Dicamay section retells Headland 2003 (Roe contacted the group on the Dicamay River near Jones, Isabela in 1957 and recorded 291 words; one family left; Headland could not find them in November 1974; Ilokano homesteaders) and discusses causes of language death. No linguistic data of any kind, no phonology, no mention of the SIL archive wordlists.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David, Jason W. Lobel & William Hall. 2023 [OUP uncorrected first proofs dated 14 Apr 2023; published 2024]. Historical linguistics of the Philippines [title on proof; cited elsewhere as 'The history of the Philippine languages']. Chapter 7 in A. Adelaar & A. Schapper (eds.), The Oxford Guide to the Malayo-Polynesian Languages of Southeast Asia. Oxford: Oxford University Press. 16 pp. proof.
sources.note: Nothing about Dicamay Agta (language not mentioned). General remarks only: Proto-Philippines is argued to have innovated phonemic/contrastive accent (Zorc 2020; Smith ch. 2), absent from Formosan and non-Philippine MP languages; no language-specific stress rule for any Northeastern Luzon Agta variety is given.

sources.citation: University of the Philippines Diliman, Department of Linguistics, The Katig Collective. c.2022-2023. Language Capsules (web series on endangered Philippine languages; 30 capsules incl. 'Adasen', 'Agta, Dicamay', 'Agta, Mt. Iriga', 'Alangan', 'Ata', 'Atta, Faire').
sources.note: no phonology; extinction history after Headland 2003/2009; points to SIL archive items 76818 (Roe 1960 wordlist) and 76709 (Isabela wordlists)

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. Table 3.2 (p.64), sec. 3.2 (p.66), sec. 3.3 (pp.96-97).
sources.note: Nothing on Dicamay stress. Lists '†Agta, Dicamay' as extinct (switched to Ilokano, population ø); p.66: 'the Agta Dicamay and the Agta of Villa Viciosa, both of which are listed by the Ethnologue as being extinct, and neither of which I have any other information about.' pp.96-97 quotes Headland 2003:7: 'SIL linguist Richard Roe contacted this group in 1957 and took a word list of 291 words.. Roe told me that there was only one family there then. In November 1974.. I was unable to find them.' — the only known primary record is that unpublished 291-word list.

sources.citation: Reid, Lawrence A. 2013. Who are the Philippine Negritos? Evidence from language. Human Biology 85(1): 329-358.
sources.note: Landing page and abstract read (digitalcommons.wayne.edu); PDF blocked (not reachable by automated download). Abstract has no Dicamay mention; a survey of Negrito group names and subgrouping, no stress data expected.

sources.note: Nothing. Fn. 2: 'two of the languages (Agta of Villaviciosa, Abra Province; Agta of Dicamay, Jones, Isabela Province) are listed as extinct' in Headland's (2002) table. No linguistic data on Dicamay.

sources.citation: Headland, Thomas N. & P. Bion Griffin. 1997. A bibliography of the Agta Negritos of Eastern Luzon, Philippines. SIL Electronic Working Papers 1997-004 (June 1997). Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics. [Glottolog ref 48923]
sources.note: Nothing. It is an enumerative bibliography (anthropology, demography, ecology, some linguistics titles such as Headland 1971 'Casiguran Dumagat [Phonological Description and Vocabulary]' and Healey 1960 'An Agta Grammar'); no linguistic description of any Agta variety, no mention of stress, accent or tone, and no entry on Dicamay Agta.

sources.citation: Roe, G. Richard (compiler). 1960. Agta - Dicamay wordlist. Handwritten entries (approx. 150 items) on the '(1966) Expanded Philippine Word List, Master List' form, 372 numbered glosses + pronoun/demonstrative prompts; sheet note 'Language: Dicamay Agta; Place: near Jones, Isabela; Date: 1960; Technician: Dick Roe'. SIL Language & Culture Archives, entry 76818 (file, 10 pp; Collection of Unpublished Materials, SIL International - Philippines; CC BY-NC-SA 3.0).
sources.note: Nothing: bare handwritten citation forms (atanan 'all', unguyutan 'to bite', me?udin 'black', digi 'blood', kolit 'bark', tiyan 'belly', manok 'bird', dila 'tongue', bubi 'woman'..) written without accent or length marks; the single exception is 201 'not' = matá (accent written, evidently to keep it apart from 96 'eye' mata). No prose, no phonology. All 10 pages viewed as images (Adobe scanned layer is garbage).

sources.citation: [SIL Philippines language-survey files; compiler not named on the sheets, data very probably G. Richard Roe's; archive dates it 1957-1980]. Isabela wordlists. Typescript 'Three Isabela word lists (Yale List..)': 219-item Yale word list in parallel columns Balla Gaddang / San Mariano Agta / Dicamay Agta, 4 pp., plus 'Yale Word List Section II' (pronouns, possessed nouns, short clauses), 1 p. SIL Language & Culture Archives, entry 76709 (Collection of Unpublished Materials, SIL International - Philippines; CC BY-NC-SA 3.0). 6-page PDF.
sources.note: No prose at all, hence no statement; but unlike Roe's handwritten sheet this typescript is a phonetic record WITH prosody marked: most Dicamay Agta forms carry an acute accent on the stressed vowel and a colon for vowel length (underlining marks a vowel quality). Read from 250-dpi renders of pp. 2-5: stress falls on the final syllable in most marked forms (limá 'hand', wigí 'left', wanán 'right', tikád 'leg', dumamá 'to walk', daddimán 'road', abú 'dust', sapáng 'back', tiyán 'belly', sagnít 'bone', digí 'blood', ulú? 'head', talingá 'ear', itán 'to see', anák 'child', asawá 'husband/wife', l…

sources.citation: Blumentritt, Ferdinand. 1893. Die Negritos am Oberlaufe des Rio Grande de Cagayan. Mitteilungen der k.k. Geographischen Gesellschaft in Wien 36: 329-331.
sources.note: Glottolog tentatively identifies these Negritos with Dicamay; a 3-page ethnographic note that may contain a few words but no stress statement. Digitized runs of the journal exist (ANNO / HathiTrust) but none was reachable by automated download.

sources.citation: Campa, Buenaventura, O.P. 1891. Una visita a las rancherias de Ilongotes (Apendice). El Correo Sino-Annamita o correspondencia de las misiones del Sagrado Orden de Predicadores en Formosa, China, Tung-king y Filipinas 25: 561-646. Manila: Imprenta del Colegio de Santo Tomas. [Negrito ('Aetas') passage pp. 584-592.]
sources.note: no phonology content. The only statement about language, p. 588: 'Su lenguaje particular es desconocido. En sus relaciones sociales con los pueblos cristianos usan el comun de la provincia, que es el ibanag; aunque tambien hablan el yogat y el gaddan, dialectos de algunas localidades.' (Their own language is unknown; with Christians they use Ibanag, also Yogad and Gaddang.) Earlier (p. c. 569, on the Ilongot) Campa likewise says the local languages are entirely unknown to him. No words recorded.
